abstract: Study distinguishing between automation-oriented and augmentation-oriented AI applications and their differential wage effects. Automation AI that replaces routine tasks tends to hurt low-skill wages by reducing demand for routine labor. In contrast, augmentation AI that enhances worker capabilities tends to raise high-skill wages by increasing the productivity and output of already-skilled workers. This dual dynamic suggests AI's wage impact depends critically on how it is deployed.
keyFindings: Automation AI hurts low-skill wages by reducing demand for routine labor
Augmentation AI raises high-skill wages by enhancing worker productivity
AI's wage impact depends critically on deployment mode (automation vs. augmentation)
The automation/augmentation distinction predicts differential effects across the skill distribution
methodology: Empirical analysis distinguishing between automation-type and augmentation-type AI deployments at the firm level, then measuring differential wage effects across the skill distribution for each deployment type.
qualifiers: The automation/augmentation distinction can be blurry in practice, with many AI tools serving both functions. Wage effects may evolve as the technology matures and deployment patterns shift. Firm-level deployment choices are endogenous to existing workforce composition.
